claim: Domain co-occurrence studied through pairwise network approaches; Wang et al. constructed Domain Co-occurrence Networks revealing scale-free properties; inherently pairwise (K=2); limited to individual proteomes.
quote: A DCN is a graph consisting of all the protein domain types of a species as nodes. Two domain types (i.e. nodes) are connected by an edge if they co-exist in one protein [26]. || We analyzed the properties of the DCNs of H. sapiens, S. cerevisiae, C. elegans, D. melanogaster, and 15 plant genomes. These DCNs have the hallmark features of scale-free networks.
grep: connected by an edge if they co-exist in one protein
whole genome protein sequences of the target organism
bib_notes: Crossref 10.1371/journal.pone.0017906: Wang Z, Zhang X-C, Le MH, Xu D, Stacey G, Cheng J; PLoS ONE 6(3):e17906, 2011. All fields match.
notes: Term used is "Protein Domain Co-occurrence Network (DCN)". Networks are built per organism ("The only input data needed for constructing a domain co-occurrence network (DCN) is the whole genome protein sequences of the target organism"), for H. sapiens, S. cerevisiae, C. elegans, D. melanogaster, 15 plant species and 398 single-chromosome prokaryotic species (wang2011.txt line 521). "Limited to individual proteomes" is accurate in the sense of one network per organism, but the study spans ~417 organisms, so consider "per-proteome" rather than "individual proteomes".

claim: Terrapon et al. used statistical co-occurrence for novel domain detection in Plasmodium falciparum, limited to pairs.
quote: To this end, all Uniprot proteins with known domain composition were used to extract domain pairs showing strong co-occurrence (as assessed by a statistical test). These domain pairs are stored in a reference list of Conditionally Dependent Pairs (CDP), which is then used as follows. || Applied to P. falciparum, our method identifies 585 new Pfam domains (versus the 3 683 already known domains in the Pfam database) with an estimated error rate below 20%.

quote: The largest set of proteins that was considered in this manner, where structures with a BLAST p-value lower than 10−80 were considered redundant, contains 32 142 protein molecules from a large variety of organisms. || Amino acids in close proximity are defined by a maximum cohesive radius of 4.5 Å for the purposes of this analysis, which corresponds to the distance between the Cα atoms of two residues that are typically considered as interacting [9].

claim: Mrzic et al. reviewed frequent subgraph mining for biomolecular data, noting that graph mining is NP-hard and scales poorly.
quote: Frequency counting is usually the most computationally intensive part of subgraph mining algorithms. || The introduction of labels into existing solutions is however non-trivial as it cause a massive explosion of the number of subgraphs that need to be evaluated. || Sometimes the graph is simply too large to be efficiently analyzed and thus the use of sampling approaches is required.
grep: most computationally intensive part of subgraph mining algorithms
massive explosion of the number of subgraphs
simply too large to be efficiently analyzed
bib_notes: Crossref 10.1186/s13040-018-0181-9: Mrzic A, Meysman P, Bittremieux W, Moris P, Cule B, Goethals B, Laukens K; BioData Mining 11(1): article 20, 2018. Matches.
notes: The review IS about frequent subgraph mining for bioinformatics (verified), but the string "NP" occurs zero times in the full text (checked in both the stripped text and the raw XML); it never says NP-hard/NP-complete and makes no general "scales poorly" statement. It only says frequency counting is computationally intensive, labels cause a "massive explosion" of candidate subgraphs, and very large graphs may need sampling. Rephrase or cite a source that states NP-hardness of subgraph isomorphism.

claim: DEAD-box helicases such as RIG-I and MDA5 are established viral RNA sensors in innate immunity.
verdict: PARTIAL: VERIFIED (viral RNA sensors) / NOT SUPPORTED (DEAD-box label)
quote: Retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)-like receptors (RLRs) are key sensors of virus infection, mediating the transcriptional induction of type I interferons and other genes that collectively establish an antiviral host response. || The three members of the RLR family have a central helicase domain and form a subfamily of SF2 helicases. || ... laboratory of genetics and physiology 2 (LGP2) — the third RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) family member — has a central DECH-box helicase domain with ATP hydrolysis activity and a carboxy-terminal domain, both involved in RNA binding and conformational rearrangements.
grep: form a subfamily of SF2 helicases
not only detect viral RNA but also cellular RNAs
bib_notes: Crossref 10.1038/s41577-020-0288-3: Rehwinkel J, Gack MU; Nature Reviews Immunology 20(9):537-551, 2020. Matches.
notes: Sensor role verified ("these proteins not only detect viral RNA but also cellular RNAs that are unusual, mislocalized or misprocessed"). The review never uses "DEAD-box" (string "DEAD" absent from the text); it classifies RIG-I/MDA5/LGP2 as having a "central DECH-box helicase domain" and as "a subfamily of SF2 helicases". The tex should say DECH-box / DExD/H-box (SF2) helicases, or RIG-I-like receptors, not DEAD-box.

claim: DEAD-box helicases co-occurring with DNA repair, recombination, replication and the SOS response are consistent with bacterial RecBCD-like repair complexes.
verdict: PARTIAL: VERIFIED (RecBCD = bacterial helicase-nuclease for DSB repair/recombination; SOS mentioned) / NOT SUPPORTED (DEAD-box link)

notes: Title itself: "RecBCD Enzyme and the Repair of Double-Stranded DNA Breaks"; also "the identification of RecBCD as a bipolar DNA helicase". SOS appears only as a recB/recC mutant phenotype ("a loss of SOS induction"), not as a described pathway. The review classifies RecB (and RecD) as superfamily 1 (SF1) DNA helicases and never mentions DEAD-box helicases (string "DEAD" absent). DEAD-box (PF00270) is an SF2 family, so "DEAD-box helicases ... consistent with RecBCD-like complexes" is not supported by this source.

bib_notes: Crossref/PubMed 10.1111/j.1574-6976.2008.00105.x: Sauvage E, Kerff F, Terrak M, Ayala JA, Charlier P; FEMS Microbiology Reviews 32(2):234-258, Mar 2008. Matches. An erratum exists: FEMS Microbiol Rev 32(3):556 (DOI 10.1111/j.1574-6976.2008.00115.x). The CSIC author-manuscript front page lists only four authors (no Kerff); the published version has five.
notes: Source: β-lactams bind the penicillin-binding (transpeptidase) domain ("PBPs are to a variable degree sensitive to β-lactam antibiotics, with which they form a stable acyl-enzyme"). The glycosyltransferase (transglycosylase) domain is described as inhibited by moenomycin, not by β-lactams. So "beta-lactam antibiotics bind these exact domains" (both PF00905 and PF00912) overstates: only PF00905 (transpeptidase) is the β-lactam target. Quotes are from the accepted author manuscript, not the typeset article.
